newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ABB 1996 profits seen lower, 1997 unspectacular.
newsitem.headline: ABB 1996 profits seen lower, 1997 unspectacular.

text.p: ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG should show solid but unspectacular earnings growth in 1997 before profit momentum returns in 1998 when Europe's battered economy finally pulls out of the doldrums, analysts said.
Earnings in 1996, which will be released on February 27, are also expected to be moderate, reflecting Europe's sluggish economy and cut-throat conditions in the power business.
"Business in 1997 will be sluggish because Europe's performance is sluggish," said Peter Gachnang of Bank Julius Baer in Zurich.

In the absence of stellar results, analysts will turn their attention to ABB's new chief executive, Goran Lindahl, who faces the daunting challenge of succeeding Percy Barnevik, one of Europe's leading industrialists and a galvanising force in ABB.
While Lindahl is unlikely to veer from the course set by Barnevik, some analysts hope he will set new profit targets when he for the first time meets the media and analysts.
"Lindahl will almost certainly have his own style, but I don't detect a significant change in direction," said Peter Knox of Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS).
Analysts expect ABB's profits in 1996 to be slightly below 1995 when results were boosted by a one-off gain of $250 million from the Adtranz transportation venture with Daimler-Benz AG.
On average 10 analysts in Zurich, Stockholm and London forecast a 1996 group net profit of $1.30 billion, 1.1 percent lower than 1995's reported $1.315 billion.
Forecasts range from $1.245 billion to $1.36 billion.
Operating profit is forecast to fall to $3.18 billion from 1995's $3.28 billion. Forecasts range from $3.1 billion to $3.267 billion.
Without the one-off payment, ABB's group net profit in 1995 was $1.065 billion so the company will still live up to its own forecast of higher profits on a comparable basis.
In 1997 ABB's net profit is forecast to rise to $1.43 billion and in 1998 to $1.71 billion.
"If things go according to plan, we should see ABB's orders rise in the second half of 1997 so growth will be better in 1998," said Angela Dean of Morgan Stanley.
Earnings in 1998 should also be helped by contributions from the transportation business and a recovery in power generation.

ABB's slowdown in 1996 and 1997 should come as no real surprise to investors, said analysts, referring to frequent warnings by ABB of the effect Europe's feeble recovery has on the company's largest segment, Industrial and Building Systems.
ABB's power generation segment is also suffering from lower earnings with most analysts expecting about a 20 percent decline in 1996 operating margins and slow rebound in 1997.

While the 10 percent rise in ABB's Swiss share since the start of this year are based on a 1998 recovery scenario, ABB's shares are often pushed higher ahead of its results in the expectation of a positive surprise.
"ABB is such a well run company that it always has the capacity to surprise," said Niall O'Connor, capital goods analysts at Credit Suisse First Boston.
Most recently, ABB's charismatic chairman, Percy Barnevik, told Reuters Financial Television in Davos that he did not have any hopes for an upturn in investment goods in 1997.

Barnevik, who stepped aside as chief executive on January 1, is respected for his views on general economic conditions and was one of the first industrialists in early 1996 to dampen expectations of a speedy recovery in Europe's economy.
Barnevik has often said that ABB follows a cycle of two bad years following three good years.
ABB, which reports in U.S. dollars but conducts more than half of its business in Europe, will also see its results negatively impacted by the recent rise in the dollar.
"There is little going aggressively right for ABB apart from continuing cost cutting," said Chris Heminway of Lehman International.
